chunks.text: A man spent about £2,500 on graphics cards, downloaded what was being called one of the best openweight coding models of the year, gave it a prompt, and got a black window with nothing rendered in it. So, he posted about it on Reddit under the title, Quen 3.8 is an Opus level. Let's not be silly. The post got downvoted to zero. On its own, that's an ordinary local AI story. New model, your own hardware, benchmark numbers that don't survive contact with your actual prompt. Then somebody else decided to reproduce exactly what he'd done. Same prompt, same black window. The failure was completely reproducible. Then he changed one thing and it wasn't the model, the quantization or the graphics card. He changed the software the model was running inside and about an hour later he had a working ocean scene with water shaders. I've been waiting for Quen 3.8 for weeks myself. And when I finally sat down with the benchmarks, the reports, and tests like that one, the story I came away with wasn't that Quen 3.8 got dramatically smarter. It was about what the same model can do once you put it inside a system that lets it work. The benchmarks are worth taking seriously, because some of the jumps are big. On Deepswe 1.1, the Aentic coding benchmark, Quen 3.6 scored 13.3 and Quen 3.8 reached 42.2. Nobody calls that incremental. Computer use on OSWorld went from 63.9 to 84.3. Those are real numbers and they're why people got excited about this release. The complication is which kind of task improved. Take GPQA Diamond which sits much closer to pure reasoning because the model doesn't get the same tool use loop there. Quen 3.6 scored 87.8 and Quen 3.8 scored 89.2. That's 1.4 points. and Quen 3.7 plus beat both of them at 90.3. So the dramatic gains aren't spread across the board. They're concentrated where the model is allowed to touch tools and behave like an agent. There's also a footnote that changes how you read the headlines. Under four of the Agentic benchmarks, including the deepsw result everyone was quoting, Quen's own model card says the evaluation was performed using the clawed code harness. The 13.3 to 42.2 to jump wasn't the model sitting there answering questions by itself. It was the model operating inside another system that handled the agent loop around it. On the same launch day, the official Quen account posted the line, "Any harness you run, the model always delivers." That got 92,000 views and 642 likes. The funny part is that Quen's own benchmark table sitting right underneath makes a decent argument that the harness does matter. That's the context the Reddit post needs. The first person setup wasn't weak. A Radeon 9,700 AI Pro with 32 GB of memory, the Unsloth Q6 build, which is a respectable quantization rather than something crushed down to nothing. A 131,000 token context window and around 29 tokens per second. The model produced a very detailed plan. Gersonner wave displacement, eight directional waves,

physically based dispersion, the actual mathematics it wanted to use. Then it built the project and the window came up black. He told the harness the screen was black and it couldn't work out what to do about that. One commenter called the plan a beautiful piece of fiction, which given there was no working ocean at the end of it is fair. The reproduction ran on an RTX5090 with around 190,000 tokens of context and roughly 150 to 160 tokens per second. He put the same prompt through VS Code Copilot and got the same black window. So far identical to the original report. Then he ran the same task on the same machine with the same weights, the same quantization, and the same prompt. This time inside DeepSeek Harness, and it worked on the first attempt. The only variable he'd changed was the harness, and his word for the difference was night and day. There's a stranger detail buried in that run. The vision pipeline wasn't wired up properly because a launch flag was missing. So, the model couldn't really see the screenshots it was supposed to be using as feedback. Instead of giving up, it wrote its own PNG decoder in the middle of the task so it could read the screenshots and check whether the water it had generated actually looked like water. Think about cooking. Same recipe, same ingredients, same cook, two different kitchens. In the first one, the cook isn't allowed to taste anything while preparing the meal. So, they can follow the recipe, but can't check the food until it's finished. In the second one, they taste it, realize something's off, adjust, taste again, and keep going until it's right. The cook hasn't become more talented. The kitchen changed what they were capable of doing. That's the gap between the two ocean runs. The first setup let the model write code but handed almost nothing back to it. Deepseek harness gave it a way to run the code, inspect what happened, notice the result was wrong, and try to fix it. When even the vision system wasn't available, it built its own way to look. That's what a harness is. the software surrounding the model that determines what it can see, which tools it can reach, how a large task gets broken into smaller pieces, and what happens when the conversation outgrows the available context. None of that lives in the weights, and all of it changes what the model can finish, which is how two people run identical weights on identical hardware and come away describing two different pieces of technology. The reasoning setting fits the same picture. Quinn gives you several reasoning effort levels and the default is set quite aggressively. Simon Willis ran a standard test prompt and found that at the default, the model spent around 21 minutes thinking before producing roughly 3,000 tokens of output with reasoning turned off, the same test took around 137 seconds. He described the default behavior as hilarious while also saying the 21-minute result was the best local result he'd ever seen.

Someone else tested the levels by asking for a Tetris clone. The lowest effort setting produced the best result. The highest one reversed all four movement keys. So, it isn't a simple more is better slider. More reasoning can help. And it can also send the model off reconsidering things that were fine the first time. The feedback loop is the more reliable improvement. If the model can run the code, inspect what happened, identify the failure, and try again, you get much more useful behavior without changing the underlying model at all, which is what makes Deep Seek Harness interesting. It's MIT licensed, the source is available, the components come as plugins, and it keeps a permanent session log, so you can resume, fork, and replay work instead of losing everything when a long session ends. There's a good example of what that looks like. One developer posted the session log of a local Quen 3.827B instance building a firstperson shooter. 687 steps, nearly 88 million tokens going in, around 822,000 coming out, roughly 5 hours of model time on two secondhand 3090s. The work itself wasn't glamorous. Write a file, run it, read the error, go back and change the file, run it again. According to him, it did that for hours while he slept. Later, he started giving it screenshots instead of only describing what he wanted, showing it the kind of gun he had in mind or the crosshair he was after. So, the images became part of the loop. His description was that he had a 27B model doing art direction with its eyes running entirely on his own hardware. That's a more useful way to think about local AI than asking which model is smarter. There's a caveat, though. Deep Sea Caress is still a developer preview, and it behaves like one. Compaction doesn't always happen at the right moment. Windows users report frequent errors. At least one developer broke their installation with a search plugin badly enough that they couldn't launch the harness anymore. The session log is what makes that survivable because the log becomes the source of truth. If the process crashes, you tell the system to resume and it continues from the existing work instead of starting over. The bigger limitation shows up when you stop building from scratch. Local models look far more impressive on a clean project than they do dropped into a medium-sized existing codebase and asked to understand what's already there. One developer had Quen 3.8 performing competitively with Frontier models on a fresh build, then gave it an existing Go and Python codebase and asked it to implement mutual TLS. It reportedly went around in circles for dozens of hours thinking through and rethinking the same problem. the same harness and the same task went much better with DeepSeek V4 running at an extremely aggressive two-bit quantization. His theory was that the smaller model couldn't build a confident enough mental picture of the existing codebase to know where to begin. So, it

kept replanning rather than committing to a solution. So, no, a 27B local model hasn't replaced every Frontier model. The realistic picture is that you might do most of a particular workflow locally and send the difficult final part to an expensive frontier model when you actually need it. What's worth noticing is how often that handoff quietly stops being necessary for a specific task once the local model has a good harness, enough context, the right tools, and a sane reasoning setting. One developer worked out that 4 hours of unattended local work would have cost him around £130 through the Opus API. That's his calculation rather than a receipt. So I wouldn't treat the exact number as universal, but the shape of it matters. A model that can work unattended for hours has very different economics from paying for every token. You don't need an expensive GPU to experiment either. Someone recently got Quen 3.827B running on an RTX 4060 with 8 GB of VRAM, around 14.6 and 6 GB on disk, a 64,000 token context, 25 layers pushed off the GPU, prefill around 150 tokens per second, and decode around five. It fits for serious agent work, it's unusable at that speed, and the difference between the model fitting and the model being usable is one of the easiest things to misunderstand when you're getting into local AI. The practical floors are more useful than the theoretical one. Around 12 GB is the theoretical minimum. things start becoming practical at 24. Around 32 is a more comfortable target since the community 4-bit versions generally land somewhere around 17 to 19 GB and the real requirement is closer to 24 once you account for cache and the context you actually use. At 48 GB, you're comfortable. At 128, you get enormous context capacity and room to run multiple instances and no extra tokens per second. On quantization, Q8 gives you the best quality and the biggest memory bill. Q6 is probably the sensible compromise for most people, and Q5 hands some of that memory back for additional context. Memory bandwidth is the part people skip. An RTX 5090 has roughly 1,792 GB per second, and people are reporting somewhere around 96 to 110 tokens per second on this model. A secondhand RTX 300090 has 24 GB of VRAM and around 1,000 GB per second. Put two together and you have 48 GB of total memory, which makes a pair of used 3090s a surprisingly attractive setup for this kind of workload. Capacity determines whether the model fits. Bandwidth has a huge influence on how fast it runs, and you can optimize for one and still be disappointed by the other. One more hardware detail. Because Quinn 3.8 8 is a dense model rather than a mixture of experts. When it spills beyond the GPU, you don't get a graceful drop in performance. You can end up with the model crawling. That's why the bigger memory machines are mostly buying you room for larger contexts or larger models rather than better generation speed. Prompt engineering tested Quen

3.8 made across two clustered DGX sparks and reported around 15 to 20 tokens per second single threaded while also pointing out that the sparks aren't really designed around running a dense 27b model. So the verdict has two halves. Taken by itself, Quen 3.827B isn't quite the upgrade the hype suggested. Better on agentic benchmarks, significantly stronger on computer use, but a small step on pure reasoning. And several of the loudest numbers came out of evaluations performed inside clawed code, which makes the surrounding harness part of the story whether you like it or not. Put the same model inside a harness that closes the feedback loop and the experience changes considerably. Same weights, same model. What changed is the system around it and that system decides whether the model can see what it did, run the result, understand the failure, and keep working until it gets somewhere useful. We've spent years reducing all of this to one question about which model is smarter. What you actually get depends on the model, the reasoning configuration, the harness, how context is managed, and which tools the model can reach. And all of those interact several axes instead of one intelligence number. And most of them are software. That's the part I find encouraging for local AI. A better model requires a new model release. A better harness doesn't. Someone can spend a Tuesday fixing the feedback loop, improving context management, adding a tool, or changing how sessions resume, and the model already sitting on your machine gets considerably more useful. The original Reddit story has a nice ending, too. The person who got the black window and the down votes came back into the thread and admitted that in this case, he'd been wrong. He said every day is a school day, and that what he'd learned was that he needed a better harness. The comment got 102 up votes, which is one of the more encouraging things I've seen online this month. The lesson isn't that Quen 3.8 magically became a Frontier model or that everyone should throw out their expensive models and run a 27B on a pair of old GPUs. It's that the model is one part of the system. If you've been judging local AI on benchmark scores and how clever the first response looks, the part you're missing is the part that decides whether it can finish the job. Better software around a model can matter as much as getting a better model. If that changed the way you think about local AI, hit the like button and subscribe for more breakdowns like this. And let me know in the comments what you're actually running. Is it a harness that gives the model a proper feedback loop, or are you still trying to cook without a spoon? I read the comments, so I'm genuinely curious what you're seeing on your own hardware.
